0.title: The Gospel and the Slave: Paul's Letter to Philemon
0.overview:
Philemon is the most personal of Paul's surviving letters — a private request from a prisoner to a friend on behalf of a runaway slave. Twenty-five verses. No doctrinal argument, no community disputes, no eschatological vision. Just a man writing to a man about a third man, in the most careful and emotionally loaded prose Paul ever produced. That it was preserved in the canon at all — and that Marcion included it in his truncated collection — tells us that the early church recognized something here that went beyond private correspondence.

The situation is this: Onesimus, a slave belonging to the wealthy Colossian Christian Philemon, had run away. By Roman law, a runaway slave was a thief — he had stolen himself, depriving his master of the economic value of his labor, and possibly taken money or property in the process (v. 18 implies some kind of financial debt). He had somehow — the details are not given — come into contact with Paul, then imprisoned in Rome (or possibly Ephesus), and had been converted. He had become genuinely useful to Paul in his imprisonment. And Paul was sending him back, letter in hand.

The letter is a masterpiece of rhetorical strategy. Paul never commands Philemon to free Onesimus — he appeals, he hints, he presses, he places moral weight. He frames Onesimus as his own child (v. 10), his very heart (v. 12), a beloved brother (v. 16). He writes a personal financial guarantee for any debt (vv. 18–19). He expresses confidence that Philemon will do 'even more than I say' (v. 21). And he announces that he is coming to stay (v. 22). By the end of the letter, Philemon cannot refuse without refusing Paul himself — and refusing Paul means refusing the gospel they both serve.

Where was Paul imprisoned? Most likely in Rome, around AD 60–62, the same imprisonment from which he wrote Colossians, carried by Tychicus with Onesimus (Col 4:7–9). Some have suggested Ephesus, which was nearer to Colossae and would make a runaway’s journey and Paul’s hoped-for visit (v. 22) easier. But Rome is where Acts leaves Paul under guard with freedom to receive visitors (Acts 28:30), and a runaway slave could hope to disappear in the capital.

The deepest theological claim of the letter is in v. 16: Onesimus is to be received 'no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother … both in the flesh and in the Lord.' The gospel does not erase social realities; it transforms them. Onesimus is still a man with a history, a legal status, a relationship with Philemon that has been damaged. But he is now a brother — in the flesh (as a human being) and in the Lord (as a fellow Christian). These two dimensions must operate simultaneously. Paul is not calling for the abolition of slavery in this letter; he is doing something more radical in the long run — he is planting a theological seed that makes slavery incompatible with Christian brotherhood.

1.title: Grace and a Brother: The Complete Letter
1.overview:
Onesimus, a slave of Philemon at Colossae, had run away, probably with some of his master’s money. In Rome he met Paul in prison and became a Christian. Paul now sends him home with this letter, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother, and to charge any debt to Paul’s account.

The letter is a model of persuasion that leaves the other person free. Paul sets aside his apostolic authority, praises what grace has already done in Philemon, and then asks him to extend it to the one person he had not counted. One word, splanchna (“heart”), runs through it (vv. 7, 12, 20). And the gospel itself is acted out: a debtor is received on the account of another, who pays what he owes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy write to Philemon, their dear fellow worker, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon’s house, with grace and peace. Philemon was a wealthy believer at Colossae, and the letter concerns his slave Onesimus, who had run away and met Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Credential He Sets Down

Paul opens not with his office but with his chains, and addresses a letter about one man's slave to the whole church in that man's house. The request will be public, among brothers, and it will be left free.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house would all hear the letter read together.

Now: Paul does not command or threaten; he makes the decision public among believers and trusts what the gospel has already done in that house.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:

Meaning first. Philemon is Paul’s shortest letter and his most personal: a single page about a runaway slave. Onesimus had fled from his master Philemon, a Christian in Colossae, perhaps after stealing from him. He met Paul in prison and became a believer, and now Paul sends him back with this letter, asking Philemon to welcome him, not as a slave but as a beloved brother. After greeting Philemon and the church in his house (vv. 1–3) and thanking God for his love and faith (vv. 4–7), Paul appeals rather than commands (vv. 8–21). Onesimus, once useless, is now useful; perhaps he was parted from Philemon for a while so that Philemon might have him back forever, as a brother. Philemon is to receive him as he would receive Paul and to charge any debt to Paul’s account, and Paul is confident he will do even more. Paul asks for a guest room (v. 22) and closes with greetings and grace (vv. 23–25). The letter is the gospel in miniature: reconciliation, substitution, and a new family in Christ that transforms the deepest social divisions. Luther said we are all Onesimus, and anyone who reads this page slowly will find himself in it: the runaway, the debtor, the one who is received on another man’s account.

The setting. Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae whose home hosted a church. He had probably been converted through Paul, perhaps in Ephesus (v. 19; Acts 19:10). Onesimus was his slave. Under Roman law, a runaway slave could be severely punished: flogged, branded, even crucified. Paul was in prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, during the same imprisonment in which he wrote Colossians and Ephesians. Tychicus carried those letters, and Onesimus travelled with him (Colossians 4:7–9). Some suggest Onesimus deliberately sought out Paul, his master’s friend, to plead his case, which was a recognised practice. However they met, Onesimus was converted.

Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus. Not an apostle. In most of his letters he opens with the office; here he sets it aside before he has written ten words. That is the first move in the most carefully constructed piece of persuasion in the New Testament. Paul is about to ask a slave owner to do something extraordinary, and he begins by laying down the one credential that could have compelled it. He will mention the authority he is not using in v. 8, and mention the chains again in v. 9. Everything in this letter is calculated to leave Philemon free. “Prisoner” (desmios) of Christ Jesus: in chains for Christ’s sake and under Christ’s control. A prisoner pleading for a slave.

And Timothy our brother. Timothy was with Paul and well known to the Colossians. A second name on a private letter about a domestic matter: Philemon is going to know that someone else has read this.

To Philemon our beloved fellow worker. “Beloved” (agapētō). “Fellow worker” (synergō). Philemon had worked with Paul in the gospel, perhaps by hosting the church, and was probably converted through him (v. 19).

And Apphia our sister. Probably Philemon’s wife. In a Roman household, the wife managed the slaves day to day, so she had a direct interest in Onesimus’s return. Paul names her as a sister: she too is being addressed as a member of the family that Onesimus has just joined.

And Archippus our fellow soldier. Perhaps Philemon’s son, and a minister in the church, the man told in Colossians 4:17 to fulfil the ministry he had received. “Fellow soldier” (systratiōtē): one who shared the battle for the gospel.

And the church in your house. “Church” (ekklēsia). The early churches met in homes; there were no church buildings until the third century (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15). The letter, though personal, was to be read to the whole church. There is the whole strategy in five words. This is not a private note. Paul has addressed a letter about one man’s slave to the entire congregation that meets in that man’s living room: the people who will be sitting there when it is read aloud, and who will watch what Philemon does next.

Christ is all, and in all. The church in Philemon’s house would hear another letter from Paul at about the same time, carried by the same messengers, and in it a sentence that this little letter puts to the test: here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all (Colossians 3:11). What gathers in Philemon’s living room is not the master’s family with his slaves at the back, but people who all belong to the same Lord. Before Paul says a word about Onesimus, the address has already named the reality he will appeal to: one church, under one Christ, meeting in one house.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter is merely a private note with no lasting value. It is inspired Scripture, revealing how the gospel transforms relationships. Nor does addressing the church mean Paul is trying to shame Philemon; it reflects that in Christ, private matters between believers are also family matters.

Isn’t addressing the whole church a kind of pressure? Yes, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. But notice the kind of pressure. He does not command, threaten, or invoke his office. He simply makes the decision public, among brothers, and trusts what the gospel has already done in this house. There is a difference between manipulation, which hides its aims and works on fear, and honest appeal, which says openly what it wants and leaves the other person free. In a church, the way a believer treats someone who has wronged him is not only his own business; it shows the family what the gospel is.

In a sentence. From Paul, a prisoner for the sake of Christ Jesus, and from our brother Timothy, to Philemon, our dear friend and co-worker, to our sister Apphia, to Archippus, who fights alongside us, and to the church that meets in your home:

On a Tuesday. Philemon’s living room was about to become the place where a slave and a master sat at one table. Open your home this month to someone your circle would not usually invite: a meal, a small group, someone in need.

For worship. The Lord Jesus became a prisoner for us before Paul was ever a prisoner for him. He was bound in a garden, led from court to court, and laid aside all his rights, so that runaways could be brought home. Every church that meets in a living room, every household where the master and the servant pray together, is a small embassy of his kingdom, where rank is laid down at the door because the King himself laid it down first.
verseByVerse.note: Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae whose home hosted the church. Apphia may have been his wife and Archippus his son. Paul wrote from prison, sending this letter with Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace to you and peace. Paul’s standard greeting, combining the Greek greeting (charis, grace) and the Hebrew (shalom, peace), and filling both with gospel meaning. In this letter it is no formality. Paul will end on the same note in v. 25: the letter is bracketed by grace, and grace is precisely what he is asking Philemon to extend. Grace is God’s undeserved favour. Philemon has received it; Onesimus has received it; and the question the letter puts is whether a man who has been dealt with on those terms can bring himself to deal with someone else the same way. Peace is the reconciliation and wholeness it brings: not the absence of conflict merely, but things put right. It is a pointed word to open a letter about a broken household. A man has run, a master has been wronged, and there may be money owing (v. 18).

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The Father and the Son together are the one source of grace and peace. “You” is plural: to the whole household and church. Paul is still speaking to the room. And there is a word in it that will do quiet work all the way through: Lord. Kyrios is the ordinary Greek for master; it is the word a slave used of the man who owned him. Philemon is Onesimus’s kyrios. Paul opens by naming a Lord above them both, and by the end he will ask Philemon to receive his slave as a brother, because they now share one. God our Father is quietly doing work too. If God is Father to Philemon and to the congregation, and Onesimus is now Paul’s child in the faith (v. 10), then the relationships in that house have already been rearranged before the argument begins. Paul lets the ordinary language of the greeting carry it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace and peace are merely polite wishes. They are blessings God gives, and they shape everything that follows.

How do I show grace to someone who has wronged me, when I do not feel gracious? Start where Paul starts: with the grace you have received. You do not manufacture grace for others out of your own reserves; you pass on what has been given to you, and you have been given more than you will ever have to give (Ephesians 4:32; Matthew 18:21–35). Feelings often follow obedience rather than leading it. So pray for the person, refuse to rehearse the wrong, speak to them kindly, and take one concrete step toward peace. Grace does not pretend the wrong did not happen, and it does not require you to trust someone who has not changed; but it does let go of the right to pay them back.

In a sentence. Grace and peace to you all from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your church or family with whom things are most broken. Pray this greeting over them by name: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Ask God what one step toward peace would look like this week.

For worship. The Father and the Son, one fountain, pour grace on people who ran from them, and make peace with rebels at their own cost. There is one Lord in every Christian household, and he is the Master who took the form of a servant; under him every master is a brother and every slave a son. Grace came first in this letter and will have the last word, as it does in the whole story of God’s dealings with runaways, and between the first word and the last every broken relationship among his people is given the possibility of being made whole.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Philemon whenever he prays, because he hears of his love for all the saints and his faith in the Lord Jesus. He prays that their shared faith will become effective as Philemon recognises every good thing they have in Christ. Philemon’s love has given Paul great joy and comfort, because the hearts of the believers have been refreshed through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Argument Built from a Man's Own Character

Paul tells Philemon truthfully what he already is, and then asks him to be it consistently. The words that describe Philemon's reputation in verse 7 — hearts and refreshed — come back in verses 12 and 20, applied to Onesimus and to the request.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon was known for his love 'for all the saints'.

Now: When you must ask something hard of another Christian, name the grace already at work in them, accurately and without flattery, and ask them to extend it to the case they had left out.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,

I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers. “My God”: a personal relationship. “Always” (pantote): Paul’s regular prayer included thanksgiving for Philemon. “You” is singular from here on: Paul now addresses Philemon personally. This thanksgiving is doing two things at once: it is sincere, and it is establishing the ground on which the request will be made.

Because I hear of your love and of the faith. “Hear” (akouōn, keep hearing) is present tense: reports kept coming. Somebody told him: perhaps Epaphras, who is with him (v. 23) and had brought news of the Colossians’ love before (Colossians 1:7–8), perhaps Onesimus himself. Love is mentioned first, perhaps deliberately, since it is love that Paul will appeal to (v. 9).

That you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints. The sentence is arranged in a crossing pattern (a chiasm): love… faith… toward the Lord Jesus… for all the saints. Faith is directed to the Lord Jesus; love to all the saints. “All the saints” is the word the whole letter turns on: every believer, including, now, Onesimus. Paul is not flattering him. He is describing him accurately and then, in a few verses, presenting him with a saint he had not counted: a man who is now among the all, and who used to serve his dinner.

The method of the letter. Paul does not begin by telling Philemon what he ought to be. He begins by telling him truthfully what he already is, and then asks him to be it consistently. That is a far harder thing to refuse than a rebuke, and it treats the man as an adult and a Christian rather than a problem to be managed.

Why faith in Christ and love for the saints belong together. Paul’s crossing sentence binds the two because the saints are not a separate object from the Lord. He had learned that on the road to Damascus, when the risen Jesus asked him, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). To harm Christ’s people was to harm Christ, and the reverse is equally true: love for the saints is faith in Christ taking hold of the people he has made his own. Jesus gave the new commandment in those very terms, that we love one another just as he has loved us (John 13:34). So when Onesimus turns up as one more of the saints, Philemon will not be asked to love a new category of person, only to see that the Lord he trusts has already claimed this one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is flattering Philemon to manipulate him. His thanks are genuine. But he is also laying a foundation: Philemon’s known love is the basis for the appeal.

How do I love all the saints, including Christians I find difficult? By remembering that the word is all, and that the reason you love them is not that they are easy but that Christ loved them. Start with prayer: it is very hard to keep resenting someone you pray for by name. Then act before you feel: greet them, ask how they are, do them a kindness. Look for evidence of grace in them and thank God for it, as Paul did for Philemon. And notice the people in your church whom you have, without meaning to, left out of your all: the new, the awkward, the poor, those from a different background. Onesimus was one of those.

In a sentence. Every time I mention you in my prayers I thank my God, because I keep hearing about your love for all of God’s people and your faith in the Lord Jesus,

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today that you thank God for their faith and love. Be specific. And if you need to raise something difficult with someone, begin, honestly, with what you see of God’s grace in them.

For worship. Faith toward the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints are what grace makes of a human being, and both are wholly God’s work. The love Philemon was known for did not begin in Colossae. It began in the heart of the Son, who, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end, the slave and the master alike, and laid down his life for each of them by name. Every report of love among believers, carried by word of mouth to a prison in Rome, is news of Christ at work in his people, and it turns rightly and at once into thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.

And I pray that the sharing of your faith. It is the most compressed sentence in the letter and the hardest to translate. “Sharing” is koinōnia: fellowship, partnership, participation, having in common. Not sharing your faith in the sense of evangelism, but the fellowship that comes from faith, the partnership Philemon has with other believers through their common faith, the shared life it produces. The word anticipates v. 17: if you consider me your partner (koinōnon).

May become effective. “Effective” (energēs) is the working word, from which we get energy: active, operative. Paul prays that Philemon’s fellowship will actually do something.

For the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. “Full knowledge” (epignōsei) is deep, experiential knowledge. “Every good thing”: every blessing and good work that belongs to us in Christ. Read it in context and the prayer is not general. The very next paragraph will present him with a specific case in which that recognition has to be exercised. He is praying, in advance, for the thing he is about to ask.

Fellowship that begins with the Son. The partnership Paul prays for has its source in a deeper one. God is faithful, he told the Corinthians, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Corinthians 1:9). Believers share a life with one another because each of them first shares in Christ: his death, his righteousness, his Spirit, his inheritance. That is what every good thing that is in us means: not a list of Philemon’s virtues but the whole wealth that belongs to believers because they are joined to Christ, and Paul prays that Philemon will know it so deeply that it overflows. A man who sees how much he has been given in Christ finds it far easier to give a runaway what he does not deserve.

For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother. “Joy” (charan) and “comfort” (paraklēsin, encouragement). Philemon’s love had brought Paul joy, even in prison. “My brother”: warm and personal. It is the warmest thing in the letter and also the most strategic.

Because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you. “Hearts” (splanchna) is literally the inward parts, the seat of deep emotion; we would say heart. Paul used it of his own longing at Philippians 1:8. “Refreshed” (anapepautai) means given rest, revived, relieved; it is what you do for an exhausted animal or a tired traveller, and the perfect tense means refreshed and still refreshed. Now watch what Paul does with these two words. In v. 12 he will call Onesimus his own splanchna, my very heart. And in v. 20 he will ask Philemon to refresh his heart in Christ, using the same two words, by refreshing Onesimus. The letter’s argument is being assembled out of the man’s own character.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Philemon’s good works earn him God’s favour. They are the fruit of faith. Nor does “the sharing of your faith” refer primarily to evangelism, though evangelism matters; it means the partnership of faith.

The King James says the communication of thy faith. Is this about evangelism? Older translations render it that way, and many have read it as a prayer for Philemon’s witness. The word means fellowship or partnership, and the more likely reading is that Paul prays for the generous partnership that flows from Philemon’s faith to bear fruit, which is exactly what he is about to ask of him. Telling others the gospel is commanded elsewhere (Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Peter 3:15), but this verse is about fellowship: the common life believers share, and what it does when it becomes active.

In a sentence. and I pray that the fellowship you have through your faith may be active and productive, as you come to understand fully every good thing we have in Christ. Your love has given me great joy and encouragement, my brother, because you have revived the hearts of God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Choose one tired believer to refresh this week, a parent, a widow, an overworked pastor, with a meal, a note, an hour of company or an offer to take the children, and let it cost you something.

For worship. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28): the Lord Jesus is the great refresher of weary hearts. He gave rest to the tired, the sick and the ashamed while he walked in Galilee, and he gives it still, often through the hands of his people. Every hot meal set before an exhausted saint, every evening of company for the lonely, is his rest passing from one heart to another. And all of it is a foretaste of the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, when every weary believer will lie down in the house of the one who refreshed them first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul could command Philemon to do what is right, but prefers to appeal in love, as an old man and now a prisoner for Christ. He appeals for Onesimus, who has become his spiritual son in prison. Onesimus, whose name means “useful”, was once useless to Philemon but is now useful to both of them. Paul is sending him back, though it is like sending his own heart. He would have liked to keep him as a helper, but wanted Philemon’s goodness to be voluntary, not forced. Perhaps Onesimus was parted from him for a while so that Philemon could have him back for ever, no longer merely as a slave but more than a slave, a dear brother, both as a man and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Goodness by Compulsion Is Not Goodness

Verse 14 governs the letter: Paul wants Philemon's goodness to be 'of your own accord'. Verse 16 is the sentence the letter exists to deliver — 'no longer as a bondservant', but a beloved brother, 'both in the flesh and in the Lord'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A runaway slave met Paul in prison and was sent home as a brother.

Now: There is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—

Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you. “Accordingly” (dio, therefore): because of Philemon’s love. “Bold enough” (pollēn parrēsian echōn) means having much boldness, freedom of speech. “Command” (epitassein) means order. Here is the hinge of the letter, and it is a masterpiece of restraint. As an apostle, Paul has authority to give orders, and he chooses not to use it. But he does not conceal the authority. He names it, so that Philemon knows exactly what is being withheld. That is not manipulation; it is the opposite of it. A man who quietly forgoes a right leaves the other person guessing. Paul puts it on the table and then sets it down where it can be seen.

To do what is required. “What is required” (to anēkon) means what is fitting, proper, your duty. Receiving Onesimus well is not optional; it is what a Christian ought to do. The outcome is not in doubt; only the manner of reaching it is.

Yet for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you. “For love’s sake” (dia tēn agapēn, because of love): either Philemon’s love or the love that binds believers. “Appeal” (parakalō) means urge, encourage, plead, call alongside. Command produces compliance; appeal produces something else, and Paul wants the something else. He will say why in v. 14: goodness by compulsion is not goodness. Paul treats Philemon as a mature believer who can respond freely.

I, Paul, an old man. “Old man” (presbytēs) means aged man. Paul was probably in his late fifties or early sixties, worn by beatings, shipwrecks and years of prison. Some scholars suggest emending it to presbeutēs, ambassador (Ephesians 6:20), but old man fits the tender appeal.

And now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus. Paul is trading on his age and his chains. Some have found this uncomfortable, as if it were emotional leverage. But there is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free. Paul is not saying you must. He is saying: this is an old man in prison, asking you. And there is something worth seeing in an apostle willing to appear as an old man rather than an office. He has spent his life insisting on his apostleship when the gospel was at stake. Here, where only a slave’s future is at stake, he lays it down without a murmur.

Lord and Teacher, with a towel. Paul’s way of naming his authority and then setting it down is not his invention. On the night before he died, Jesus took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then said, You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (John 13:13). He named his authority, and used it to kneel. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet (13:14). Paul the apostle, appealing as an old man in chains, is a servant following his Master, and he is asking Philemon to do the same: to use his rights as a master to stoop to a slave.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s authority was weak or optional. He had it, and mentions it. It means love is the better way to motivate believers when possible. Nor is this manipulation; it is honest and transparent.

When should a parent, leader or elder command rather than appeal? Command when the matter is clear, urgent or dangerous, or when appeal has been refused: a child running into the road needs an order, not an invitation, and Paul himself gave firm commands where the gospel or the church’s purity was at stake (2 Thessalonians 3:6; 1 Corinthians 5). But wherever you can, appeal. Explain why, show the person what love and the gospel ask, and let them choose. That is how you grow mature believers rather than compliant ones. Authority that is always used is soon resented; authority that is held in reserve and laid down in love is rarely needed.

In a sentence. So, although in Christ I could be bold and order you to do what you ought, I would rather appeal to you on the basis of love. I, Paul, an old man and now also a prisoner for Christ Jesus,

On a Tuesday. If you have authority over others (as a parent, manager, or leader), where could you appeal in love rather than simply command? Choose one instruction you would normally give this week and turn it into an appeal: explain the reason, say what you hope for, and leave room for a willing yes.

For worship. God has every right to command, and he does command; yet over and over he pleads. Come now, let us reason together. Return to me. Be reconciled to God, his ambassadors implore on behalf of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20). The Lord of glory, who could summon his creatures to obedience with a word, became the man of sorrows and stood at the door and knocked. He wins his people not by force but by love, until they come willingly in the day of his power (Psalm 110:3), and the yes he receives from them is the free yes he wanted all along.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)

I appeal to you for my child. “My child” (tou emou teknou). Note the order of the Greek: the appeal, the relationship, and only then the name. The first word Philemon hears about his runaway slave is that he is Paul’s child. By the time the name lands, the name of the man who had run, Paul has already claimed him as a son.

Onesimus. Onesimus was Philemon’s slave who had run away. His name means useful or profitable, a common slave name, given for the obvious reason.

Whose father I became in my imprisonment. “Became father” (egennēsa) means begot, gave birth to. Paul led Onesimus to Christ while in chains. Spiritual fatherhood (1 Corinthians 4:15; Galatians 4:19). And the runaway got as far as Rome, the obvious place to disappear in a city of perhaps a million, and there met the one man in the empire most likely to send him home. Whatever Onesimus thought he was doing, God used Paul’s imprisonment and Onesimus’s flight to bring him to salvation.

Formerly he was useless to you. A wordplay: Useful (Onesimus) was useless (achrēston). Perhaps an admission that Onesimus had been a poor slave. Possibly also a play on Christos: he was without Christ (a-chrēstos may have sounded like a-christos in the pronunciation of the time). The wordplay is gentle, and it is an admission. Paul does not pretend the man was a good servant badly treated. He was useless, and Paul says so, and v. 18 allows that he may owe money besides. That candour is essential to the letter’s integrity. Paul is not asking Philemon to pretend nothing happened or to accept a rewritten history. He concedes the whole charge, and then asks for the man anyway, on entirely different grounds.

But now he is indeed useful to you and to me. “Useful” (euchrēston) means very useful, serviceable, and to some ears it may have sounded like good Christ. Conversion has made him what his name said. Paul has found him genuinely useful in prison, and expects Philemon to find the same. Grace does not only forgive a man’s past; it makes him worth something, and Paul is prepared to put his own experience of the man behind the claim. Grace transforms people and makes them useful (2 Timothy 2:21; 4:11, where the same word is used of Mark).

Useful because he is in Christ. What made the difference between the useless slave and the useful brother? Onesimus had been joined to Christ. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, behold, the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Lord who had taken the form of a servant now lived in a servant, and the honesty, diligence and faithfulness Paul found in him were Christ’s own life taking shape in a runaway. That is why Paul can promise Philemon something he has never seen: a slave worthy of his name.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conversion automatically erases the consequences of past wrongs. Paul addresses the debt (v. 18). But it does mean a new person stands before Philemon (2 Corinthians 5:17).

How do I know whether someone who wronged me has really changed? Look for the fruit Paul could point to. Onesimus did not merely say he was sorry: he came back to face the man he had wronged, he did not hide the debt, and he had proved himself in service over time. Real repentance owns the wrong without excuses, seeks to put right what can be put right, and shows itself in changed behaviour that lasts (Luke 19:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). Forgiveness can be given at once; trust is rebuilt over time. You may forgive fully and still wait, wisely, to see the fruit before handing back responsibility.

In a sentence. appeal to you on behalf of my son Onesimus, who became my child in the faith while I was in chains. Once he was of no use to you, but now he really is useful, both to you and to me.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have written off as useless: a colleague, a relative, a former friend who let you down? Pray for them by name this week. The God who made a runaway slave into a beloved son has not changed, and he may be at work in them in ways you cannot see.

For worship. We were all once achrēstos, without Christ and of no use to God, and none of us went looking for him. He came after us. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and he follows runaways down every road they take, into the great cities of the world and the far corners of their own hearts, until he finds them, often in the last place they expected to meet him. Then he makes them his children and gives them a name and a usefulness they could never have earned. A slave who ran from his master ran straight into the arms of his Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was Philemon’s slave who had run away. His name means “useful,” and Paul plays on it.

verseByVerse.quote: I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.

I am sending him back to you. Three words in the Greek that decide everything, and they come before any of the pleading. “Sending back” (anepempsa) means sent up, sent back, and it is also used of referring a case to a higher authority. Paul does not hide Onesimus, or argue that his conversion has cancelled the legal position, or ask Philemon to waive his claim from a safe distance. He puts the man on the road to Colossae with a letter in his hand. Under Roman law a returning fugitive could be branded, flogged, or worse, and both men knew it. The whole appeal is made after the risk has already been taken. Onesimus also showed courage and repentance in returning, facing possible punishment.

Sending my very heart. “My very heart” (ta ema splanchna) means my own inward parts: the word from v. 7. Philemon refreshes the hearts of the saints; Paul is sending him his own. To receive Onesimus is to receive Paul’s heart; to harm him is to harm Paul, in a place he has named.

I would have been glad to keep him with me. “Would have been glad” (eboulomēn) means I was wishing, I wanted. Paul wanted him and says so plainly. There is no pretence that returning him was easy or that Onesimus was dispensable.

In order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel. “On your behalf” (hyper sou) is delicate. Paul tactfully suggests that Onesimus’s service would have been Philemon’s gift to Paul, which quietly proposes a way for a slave owner to be generous rather than merely deprived, and hints that Philemon might send Onesimus back to serve Paul.

But I preferred to do nothing without your consent. “Consent” (gnōmēs) means judgement, opinion, approval. Onesimus belonged to Philemon under law. Paul would not take advantage.

In order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord. “Goodness” (to agathon sou) is your good deed. “By compulsion” (kata anankēn) means under pressure. “Of your own accord” (kata hekousion) means voluntarily, freely. This is the sentence that governs the whole letter. Paul could have kept him. He could have written a letter Philemon could not refuse. He did neither, and the reason is stated as a principle: good done under compulsion is not truly good. It has the shape of the thing and none of the substance (2 Corinthians 9:7). That is why this letter argues instead of commanding, and it is a considerable statement about how God deals with people. He could compel outward conduct and often does not, because what he is after is not conduct alone but a willing heart, and compulsion cannot produce one.

Freely, as he gave himself. The principle Paul will not break, that goodness must be free, is rooted in the cross. Nobody compelled the Son of God. He said of his life that no one took it from him, that he laid it down of himself and had authority to take it up again (John 10:18), and Paul could say of him, he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). So Paul will not extract a forced kindness from him, because a gospel of free grace cannot be answered with grudging compliance. What he wants from Philemon is what Christ gave Philemon: goodness entirely of its own accord.

What it does not mean. Sending Onesimus back does not mean Paul approved of slavery. He worked within the legal realities while transforming the relationship from within (v. 16). Nor does it mean Paul was indifferent to Onesimus’s danger; he provided a letter of protection and his own guarantee.

Did not the law forbid returning a runaway slave to his master? Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbade Israel to hand back a slave who had escaped to them from his master. That law protected foreign slaves escaping to Israel from cruel masters. Paul is sending a brother back to a fellow believer, with a letter that asks him to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself (v. 17), so that Onesimus goes back to a changed household, not to punishment. Sadly, slaveholders in later centuries cited this letter to justify returning fugitive slaves; they ignored everything the letter actually asks.

Should a new Christian go back and face the consequences of past wrongs? Often, yes. Conversion cancels guilt before God, but it does not cancel just obligations to people. Zacchaeus repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8); Onesimus went back. A believer who has stolen should repay where he can; one who has committed a crime may need to confess it to the authorities; one who has wronged a family member should seek them out. Do it wisely, with counsel from your pastor, especially where there are legal implications or where the person wronged might be harmed by contact. The aim is not to earn forgiveness, which Christ has already won, but to walk in the light and put right what can be put right.

In a sentence. I am sending him back to you, and in sending him I am sending my own heart. I would have liked to keep him here with me, so that he could serve me in your place while I am in chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your agreement, so that any kindness you show would be your own free choice, not something forced.

On a Tuesday. Is there a wrong you need to put right, as Onesimus did by returning? Take the hard step this week, trusting God with the outcome. And if you are the one waiting to see whether someone will do the right thing, give them room to do it freely.

For worship. The Father sent his very heart into a hostile world, his own beloved Son, knowing exactly what it would cost, and he did not hide the risk. The Son came gladly, and when the hour arrived he set his face to go to Jerusalem. No one dragged him to the cross. And because his gift was free, the obedience he works in his people is free as well. He does not drag them into goodness; he wins them, and every willing kindness they show is truly theirs and wholly his.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while. “Perhaps” (tacha): Paul does not claim certain knowledge of God’s purposes, but suggests them humbly. The perhaps is exquisite. Paul is offering Philemon a way of reading his own loss, and he does not claim to know the mind of God about a theft in Colossae. And notice the passive: “he was parted” (echōristhē), was separated. Paul does not say he ran away, which would emphasise Onesimus’s sin and is what happened, but was parted, hinting at God’s hidden hand. It is the same delicacy as Joseph telling his brothers that God sent him to Egypt (Genesis 45:5–8) without pretending they had not sold him: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God’s providence works even through human sin, without excusing it.

That you might have him back forever. “Have back” (apechēs) means receive in full, possess completely. “For a while” is literally for an hour, set against “forever” (aiōnion, eternally). A few months of loss set against an eternity of brotherhood: Paul is asking Philemon to do the arithmetic.

No longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant. Verse 16 is the sentence the whole letter exists to deliver, and it should be read carefully, because Paul does not quite say what we might wish he said. He does not command manumission. He says something that is in the long run more corrosive: whatever Onesimus’s legal status, the category has been superseded. “No longer as” (ouketi hōs): the relationship is transformed. He may still be legally a slave, but Philemon can no longer regard him merely as a slave. “More than a bondservant” (hyper doulon, above a slave).

As a beloved brother. “Brother” (adelphon). The heart of the letter. In Christ, master and slave are brothers, equal members of God’s family (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). This idea, if taken seriously, would ultimately dissolve slavery.

Brothers because of the firstborn. Where does a brotherhood strong enough to outlast slavery come from? From the Son. Christ is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Onesimus and Philemon became brothers the day each became Christ’s, because each was adopted into the same family through the same elder Brother. That is why it is forever: it does not depend on how Philemon feels about his slave, or on what Roman law says about him; it depends on Christ, who will never disown either of them. A master who refused to treat Onesimus as a brother would be refusing the very relationship on which his own salvation rested.

Especially to me, but how much more to you. Onesimus is dear to Paul; he should be even dearer to Philemon, who had known him for years.

Both in the flesh and in the Lord. “In the flesh”: in ordinary human relationships, as a member of his household, in the actual house, in the daily arrangements, not merely in some spiritual realm where equality costs nothing. “In the Lord”: as a fellow believer. Paul will not let the brotherhood be confined to Sunday. The gospel changes not only spiritual relationships but everyday ones.

Where Christians differ: did Paul want Onesimus freed? Some think Paul was silently content for Onesimus to remain a slave; others think he was hinting strongly at freedom. Verdict: Paul does not explicitly demand freedom, but “no longer as a bondservant,” “more than a bondservant,” “receive him as you would receive me” (v. 17), and “you will do even more than I say” (v. 21) all point strongly in that direction. Early tradition suggests an Onesimus later became bishop of Ephesus; if this is the same man, Philemon presumably freed him. More importantly, Paul establishes the principle of brotherhood that makes slavery incompatible with the gospel.

Does the Bible, then, condone slavery? No. Paul’s silence about abolition is not approval. He worked within a society where slavery was everywhere and could not be changed by a letter, but he planted what would destroy it: a slave is a beloved brother, Paul tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Roman slavery was also not identical to the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, which began with man-stealing, a crime the law of Moses punished with death (Exodus 21:16). Christian abolitionists in later centuries drew on exactly these truths. The gospel did not overthrow slavery by decree; it made it impossible for those who believed it. It is something a slave society could not survive being told: that the man in the kitchen is your brother, in the house as well as in the assembly. Where that was believed, the institution eventually became unthinkable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God approves of Onesimus’s running away, or any sin. God’s providence uses sin without endorsing it. Nor does it mean every hardship comes with a visible purpose; Paul says “perhaps.”

How should I read God’s providence in my own losses? With Paul’s perhaps. You may be sure that God works all things for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and you may sometimes see, looking back, what he was doing. But you will not always see it, and you must never use providence to excuse a wrong, your own or someone else’s. Joseph’s brothers were still guilty; Onesimus still owed his master. Hold both: the sin was real, and God was not absent from it. And be slow to explain other people’s suffering to them. Offer a perhaps, gently, only if it comforts.

In a sentence. Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a short time was so that you could have him back for good, no longer as a slave, but as something far better than a slave: a dear brother. He is especially dear to me, but even more so to you, both as a member of your household and as a brother in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your life whose relationship to you is defined mostly by role: the cleaner, the employee, the boss, the carer, the person who serves your coffee. If they are a believer, they are your brother or sister forever; if not, they bear God’s image. Treat them that way this week, by name, as more than their role.

For worship. God is the Lord of the perhaps. He turned a brother’s betrayal in Canaan into the saving of nations, a slave’s flight from Colossae into a son’s homecoming, and the darkest injustice ever done, the cross, into the redemption of the world. He never excuses the sin he overrules, and he never wastes it. He makes slaves into brothers and strangers into family forever, and in his hands the losses of an hour become gains for eternity. For a while his people may be parted; in him they are given back to one another for good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Philemon counts Paul a partner, he should welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul. If Onesimus has done him any wrong or owes him anything, Philemon should charge it to Paul’s account; Paul writes in his own hand that he will repay it, not to mention that Philemon owes Paul his very self. Paul asks for this benefit in the Lord, to refresh his heart, confident that Philemon will do even more than he asks. He asks Philemon to prepare a guest room, hoping to be released through their prayers. Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke send greetings, and Paul ends with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charge That to My Account

Verses 17-19 enact the gospel rather than explain it: a debt is taken on by another, in writing, and the debtor is to be received 'as you would receive me'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Welcoming a runaway slave to his table would cost Philemon standing among the slave-owning households of Colossae.

Now: Paul asks for more than private forgiveness and then promises to come and see (v. 22). Reconciliation that must be explained face to face is harder to leave half-done.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.

So if you consider me your partner. This is the request. Everything before it has been preparation and everything after is detail, and it is one sentence long. “Partner” (koinōnon) means sharer, companion, fellow in a partnership, related to koinōnia in v. 6, where Paul prayed that the sharing of Philemon’s faith would become effective. A partner in the ancient world was someone with whom you held things in common, often in business; and Paul is invoking a relationship Philemon would certainly acknowledge in order to draw a conclusion he might not. The if is not doubt but appeal: the Greek assumes it is true, since you consider me your partner. He is not asking whether Philemon will obey an apostle. He is asking what a partnership is worth when it becomes expensive.

Receive him as you would receive me. “Receive” (proslabou) means welcome, accept, take to yourself. It is the word Paul uses of how Christ received us: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you (Romans 15:7). Not forgive him. Not merely take him back. Receive him as Paul, with the welcome, the seat, the standing that an apostle and old friend would be given if he walked through the door. Paul stands in for Onesimus; to receive one is to receive the other.

What it would cost. A slave who has wronged his owner and run is to be welcomed home as though he were the most honoured guest the house could receive. There is no half-measure available; Paul has named the standard and it is himself. Philemon has other slaves, and they will be watching. He has neighbours who own slaves, and they will hear. A master who welcomes a runaway to his own table has, in the eyes of every household in Colossae, lost control of his, and there was no mechanism in that society for such a man to be admired for it. Paul is not asking for a private act of forgiveness. He is asking Philemon to accept a public humiliation.

The deeper pattern. And there is a deeper pattern in it, which the New Testament makes explicit elsewhere. One stands in the place of another, and the offender is received on the standing of the one who intercedes. Philemon is being asked to accept Onesimus on Paul’s account, which is precisely how Philemon himself was accepted. It is a picture of how Christ presents us to the Father, and the Father receives us as he receives his Son. We are accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Onesimus had Paul’s apostolic authority. It means he should receive the same welcome and love.

Does receiving a repentant person mean ignoring past harm? No. Receiving is welcome, not amnesia. Onesimus’s debt was faced, not denied (v. 18). In a church, a repentant brother is welcomed back to fellowship, to the Lord’s table and to friendship. But where the wrong involved abuse, violence or danger to others, love for the vulnerable still governs: the church must report crimes to the authorities, protect those at risk, and may rightly place limits on where and how the person serves, however sincere his repentance. Forgiveness restores a brother to the family; it does not require placing him where he could harm someone again. Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden in the name of grace.

In a sentence. So if you count me as your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.

On a Tuesday. Who is the person your church would find hardest to welcome: the former prisoner, the one who left in anger and has come back, the newcomer from a background that makes people uneasy? Decide this week to receive one such person as you would receive your most honoured friend: sit with them, invite them home, learn their name.

For worship. We came to the Father’s door as runaways, with nothing to offer and a debt behind us, and found the door already open. The Son stood beside us and spoke for us, and we were given not the servants’ entrance but the welcome of the house: the place at the table, the robe and the ring, the honour that belongs to him. No one has ever been received more lavishly than a sinner received for Christ’s sake. Every welcome a believer gives a returning brother is a small overflow of that one.

verseByVerse.quote: If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.

If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything. “Wronged” (ēdikēsen) means did injustice. “Owes” (opheilei) means is in debt. The if is most likely a courtesy. Runaway slaves did not generally travel to Rome without funds. Onesimus may have stolen money when he fled, and his absence had cost Philemon his labour. Paul concedes the wrong without dwelling on it, and then does the only thing that actually resolves it.

Charge that to my account. “Charge to my account” (emoi elloga) means reckon to me, put it on my ledger: a commercial accounting term. Paul is not asking Philemon to absorb the loss or to be big about it. He is offering to pay. Luther wrote that we are all Onesimuses: as Paul took on Onesimus’s debt so that Philemon would receive him, so Christ took on our debt so that the Father would receive us. This is the logic of double imputation: our sin was charged to Christ’s account, and his righteousness is credited to ours (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 4:6–8). The theology in this is impossible to miss, and Paul does not point at it. A man who owes a debt he cannot pay; a third party who assumes it in writing at his own cost; and the offended party asked to receive the debtor as though he were the one who paid. Paul has spent his letters arguing that doctrine, and here he simply does it, in a domestic matter, for a single man.

I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it. “Write with my own hand” (egrapsa tē emē cheiri): Paul took the pen from his secretary and wrote a legal promissory note, a binding IOU. “I will repay” (egō apotisō) means I will pay in full, a legal term for paying compensation. It is a formal, enforceable promise, written into a letter the whole church will hear read.

To say nothing of your owing me even your own self. “To say nothing” (hina mē legō, not to mention) is a rhetorical device: saying something by claiming not to say it. It is the lightest touch in the letter. Paul has just offered to pay a debt to Philemon, and mentions, while insisting he is not mentioning it, that Philemon owes him everything. Paul probably led Philemon to Christ, perhaps during his years in Ephesus (Acts 19:10). Philemon owes Paul his spiritual life. Any debt Onesimus owes Philemon is small next to what Philemon owes Paul. It is done with a smile, and it is unanswerable. What is a household debt against a man’s own soul?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thought Philemon was forced to forgive the debt. He offers to pay it, but also hints that Philemon might cancel it out of gratitude. Nor does the picture of imputation mean Paul’s payment saves Onesimus; it is an illustration of what Christ does, not a parallel saving act.

What does it mean that my debt was charged to Christ? It means that every sin you have committed, against God and against others, was entered on Christ’s account and paid in full at the cross (Isaiah 53:5–6; Colossians 2:13–14). God does not pretend your debt never existed; he transferred it to his Son, who bore its whole penalty. And in exchange, Christ’s perfect obedience is credited to you, so that God receives you as righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:19). This is why a believer can have peace with God even on his worst day. The account is not settled by your improvement but by his payment, and it is settled forever.

Does forgiving someone mean cancelling every debt and every consequence? Forgiveness means giving up the right to take revenge and to hold the wrong against the person; it does not always mean every practical debt disappears. Paul does not pretend the money is not owed; he arranges for it to be paid. Sometimes love will cancel a debt outright, as Philemon perhaps did. Sometimes repayment is right and good for the one who did wrong. And where the law has been broken, the courts may still have their say (Romans 13:4). What forgiveness forbids is bitterness, grudge-keeping and personal vengeance.

In a sentence. If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, put it on my bill. I, Paul, am writing this in my own handwriting: I will pay it back. And I won’t mention that you owe me your very self.

On a Tuesday. Is someone in your debt, in money, in hurt, in an apology never given? Ask God whether this is a debt to cancel, as you have been forgiven far more. And if you owe someone, do not wait for them to raise it. Settle it this week.

For worship. The Son of God looked at a debt no sinner could ever pay and took it as his own. He did not write an IOU and promise to settle later; he paid in full, with his own blood, on a cross outside Jerusalem. The record of debt that stood against us, with its legal demands, he set aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14): a sentence written to the very town where Philemon kept his accounts. And we, who owe him our very selves, are not sent a bill. We are received as sons.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably led Philemon to Christ, perhaps during his years at Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.

Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. “Yes, brother”: and the word matters, because it is the very term he has just asked Philemon to apply to Onesimus (v. 16). Paul, Philemon and Onesimus are now all in the same category, and the letter has quietly put them there. “Benefit” (onaimēn) means may I have profit, joy, help, and it plays once more on the name Onesimus, useful: it is from the same root. Paul is punning again: let me have some Onesimus from you. Even here, at the close, the argument is being made in the man’s name.

Refresh my heart in Christ. “Refresh” (anapauson) and “heart” (splanchna) are the same words as v. 7. Philemon refreshes the hearts of the saints; now let him refresh Paul’s. And since Onesimus is Paul’s very heart (v. 12), refreshing Onesimus refreshes Paul. Paul asks for the thing this man is already famous for, in the one case where it will cost him.

Confident of your obedience, I write to you. “Obedience” (hypakoē). Though Paul appealed rather than commanded (vv. 8–9), he still expects obedience. To obey the apostle’s word is to obey Christ.

Knowing that you will do even more than I say. “Even more” (hyper ha legō) means beyond what I say. What could be more than receiving Onesimus as a brother? Every commentator has wondered, and the obvious candidate is freedom: most likely freeing him, and perhaps sending him back to serve Paul in the gospel. Paul has carefully not asked for manumission; he asked for a brother to be received as a brother, and here he leaves a door open without walking through it. He will not name it, because naming it would make it a command and destroy the very thing v. 14 insisted on: goodness freely given.

At the same time, prepare a guest room for me. “Guest room” (xenian) means lodging, hospitality. Paul hopes to be released and to visit. It is the gentlest possible pressure. Whatever Philemon decides, the apostle expects to walk into that house and see how it turned out. It is said warmly and as a hope resting on their prayers, and it is also, unmistakably, an accountability. A decision you will have to explain to someone’s face is a different decision from one you make at a distance.

For I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you. “Your prayers” is plural (hymōn): the whole church’s prayers. “Graciously given” (charisthēsomai) means freely granted as a gift of grace. Paul believes prayer matters to his release, though the outcome is God’s gift. He was in fact released, it seems, after this imprisonment.

In the Lord, in Christ. Twice in one verse Paul names the sphere where all this happens: benefit in the Lord, refreshment in Christ. Everything he has asked runs through Christ. Philemon is being asked to act as a man who lives in Christ, toward a brother who lives in Christ, for an apostle whose heart is in Christ. That is also why Paul can be confident. The obedience he expects is not finally to himself. It is obedience to the Lord who had already made Philemon what he was, and who can be trusted to carry the good work he began in him beyond anything Paul dared to ask (Philippians 1:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was manipulating Philemon with the threat of a visit. It is a natural and warm expression of hope. Nor does it mean prayer forces God’s hand; God answers as a gracious gift.

Was Paul released, and did he visit? He expected to be released (compare Philippians 1:25), and the early church believed he was released from his first Roman imprisonment and travelled again before his final arrest; the Pastoral Letters fit that picture (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5; 2 Timothy 4:13, 20). Whether he reached Colossae, Scripture does not say. What we do know is that he hoped to, and that he expected the prayers of a small house church to be part of how God would answer.

In a sentence. Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. I write this confident that you will do what I ask, and I know you will do even more. And one more thing: get a guest room ready for me, because I hope that in answer to your prayers I will be given back to you.

On a Tuesday. If you have forgiven someone, look for the extra step: the invitation, the gift, the public word of welcome that makes the forgiveness visible.

For worship. God always does more than he says. He promised a seed to Abraham and gave him a multitude; he promised Israel a land and gave the nations a Saviour; he promised forgiveness and gave adoption, an inheritance, and the Spirit as a guarantee. He is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20), and the gospel is the story of a God who went beyond what anyone dared to ask. The even more Paul hoped for from Philemon is a small, human echo of the even more that runs through everything God gives.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefit” (onaimēn) plays once more on the name Onesimus, “useful.”

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you. Five names, and they are the same circle that appears at the close of Colossians (Colossians 4:10–14), which is one of the reasons the two letters are thought to have travelled together, carried by Tychicus with Onesimus walking beside him (Colossians 4:7–9). Epaphras founded the church at Colossae (Colossians 1:7) and wrestled in prayer for them (Colossians 4:12–13). “Fellow prisoner” (synaichmalōtos) means fellow captive: perhaps literally imprisoned with Paul, or voluntarily sharing his confinement.

And so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. Mark, the deserter of Acts 15:38, now restored (2 Timothy 4:11). Aristarchus, from Thessalonica, who had travelled and suffered with Paul (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Demas, who is still faithful here, and who would later desert Paul for love of this world (2 Timothy 4:10). Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), who would be the last one with him (2 Timothy 4:11). These are witnesses, and the list is affectionate and it is also, like everything else in this letter, quietly public. And it is a sobering list: Mark was restored; Demas would fall. Faithfulness today does not guarantee faithfulness tomorrow, except by grace.

Grace be with your spirit. “Your” is plural: to the whole church, the whole household, everyone in that room. “With your spirit”: with your inner being. And Paul has defined this grace elsewhere: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The letter began with that grace (v. 3) and ends with it, which is exactly right, because grace is what the letter has been asking for from beginning to end: that a man made rich by another’s poverty, and received without deserving it, should spend something of himself to receive somebody else the same way. Grace is what Paul asks Philemon to show, because grace is what Philemon has received.

What happened? We are never told what Philemon did. The letter’s survival is itself the strongest evidence: a document recording a request that had been refused would hardly have been copied and treasured by the church that heard it read. There is a further hint, though it can be put no higher. Some fifty years later Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the church at Ephesus in warm praise of their bishop, a man named Onesimus, and he plays on the name with the very verb of v. 20: may I have joy of you (onaimēn). Whether it is the same man cannot be proved, and the name was common enough. But it is a pleasant thought that the runaway ended his life as a bishop, and that the letter asking for his welcome was kept safe by the churches he served.

What it does not mean. Demas’s presence here does not mean he was already false; he was a genuine co-worker at the time. His later desertion is a warning, not a judgement on this moment.

Could I fall away like Demas? Demas is a warning that outward service, even at an apostle’s side, does not prove a heart that will endure. Those who finally abandon Christ show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). But a true believer will be kept: the Lord who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). The way he keeps us is through warnings like this one, which drive us back to him. So do not presume, and do not despair. If you fear falling, that fear is itself a sign of life; take it to Christ, guard against love for this present world, stay close to his people, and lean on his grace, which held Mark after his failure and can hold you.

In a sentence. Epaphras, who shares my imprisonment for Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, and so do my fellow workers Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

On a Tuesday. Write the names of four or five Christians you work alongside in the gospel, in your church, your family or your mission. Pray for each by name this week, that they will stay faithful to the end, and send one of them a word of thanks.

For worship. The grace that restored Mark after his failure, turned Onesimus from a runaway into a brother, and softened a slave owner’s heart in Colossae is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and it rests on his people still. Demas’s story is a warning, but the last word of the letter is not Demas; it is grace, and grace keeps what it has bought. It opened this little letter and it closes it, and it will close the story of every one of his people: received on another’s account, debts paid, brothers forever, home at last.
verseByVerse.note: The same companions greet the Colossians.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker<sup>2</sup>and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers,<sup>5</sup>because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,<sup>6</sup>and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ.<sup>7</sup>For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.<sup>8</sup>Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required,<sup>9</sup>yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—<sup>10</sup>I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment.<sup>11</sup>(Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)<sup>12</sup>I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart.<sup>13</sup>I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel,<sup>14</sup>but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.<sup>15</sup>For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever,<sup>16</sup>no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.<sup>17</sup>So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.<sup>18</sup>If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.<sup>19</sup>I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.<sup>20</sup>Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.<sup>21</sup>Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.<sup>22</sup>At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.<sup>23</sup>Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you,<sup>24</sup>and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.<sup>25</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
